# Building the Factory, Not the Feature: How I Work with AI Agents

2026-11-25 | Tags: AIAgents, SoftwareEngineering, DeveloperExperience

A year ago most of my time went into typing code. Now most of it goes into the system that produces the code.

That shift is easy to describe badly. "AI writes the code now" is wrong in the ways that matter. The agent writes a draft. Whether that draft becomes a working change depends on everything around it: what the agent knew before it started, what it was allowed to touch, how it found out it was wrong, and what it left behind for the next session.

I have started calling that surrounding system the **software factory**. This post is about how I build it, and what I have learned running it across a dozen personal repositories.

---

## The agent is the cheapest part of the line

A factory has inputs, stations, quality gates, and outputs. Mapped onto agent work:

- **Inputs** are intent and context: what I want, and what the agent has to know to do it.
- **Stations** are agents, often several in parallel, each with a narrow job.
- **Quality gates** are typechecks, tests, builds, and smoke checks against the real thing.
- **Outputs** are a commit and a written record of what changed and why.

The model is the most impressive part of this picture and the least interesting to optimise. It gets better every few months without me doing anything. The inputs, gates, and outputs are mine, and they decide whether a fast model produces fast progress or fast mess.

---

## 1. Context is written down once

Every agent session starts cold. Whatever it does not read, it does not know.

So the rules for how I work live in one file, `AGENTS.md`, at the root of my workspace. It is short on purpose. A few lines from it:

- If you have to wait, start a background task and do something productive.
- Split independent work across parallel subagents.
- Whatever we test manually first should get an automated test.
- Keep session docs in `~/dev/personal/docs`.
- Each repo is its own clone, with no parent repo. Use `mani` for cross-repo git and never assume a single repo root.

That last rule exists because an agent got it wrong. Every rule in the file traces back to a mistake I did not want to correct twice.

I use more than one agent tool, and they each look for a different filename. Rather than keep copies in sync, `CLAUDE.md` contains a single line, `@AGENTS.md`. One source of truth means one place to fix things.

---

## 2. Every session leaves a document

The most useful habit I have picked up is that every non-trivial session ends with a dated markdown file: `2026-11-10-termux-media-box-audit-followups.md`, `2026-11-23-claude-code-opencode-parity.md`, and so on. There are more than forty of them now.

Each one answers the same questions:

- What changed, and in which files?
- How was it verified? (Which commands, and what passed.)
- What is still open?
- What surprised us? (The gotcha that cost twenty minutes.)

These documents are written for two readers. One is me in three months. The other is the next agent, which can read the last session's notes instead of rediscovering the codebase. Notes tie the factory together across days. Without them, every session is a new hire's first morning.

A status line at the top helps more than I expected. "**Status (2026-11-11): implemented.**" tells the next reader immediately whether they are looking at a plan or a record.

---

## 3. A manual check is a test that hasn't been written yet

Agents are very good at producing code that looks right. The defence is not reading harder. It is making "right" something a machine can check.

My rule: if I checked something by hand, an automated test should exist for it afterwards. On my home media server, the music player was only ever tested by me clicking around. One audit pass replaced that with a small DOM harness: a fake `document`, `Audio`, `localStorage`, and `fetch`, around 240 lines, importing the real modules and checking that next and previous wrap at both ends, that play requests the right URL, and that the queue renders.

The test count went from 65 to 78 in that batch. More importantly, the next agent that touches the player gets told immediately when it breaks something, instead of me finding out on the sofa.

A related lesson: **audit twice.** The first audit on that project found small races and two test gaps, and all of it got fixed. The second audit then found the gaps the fixes had left behind. Agent-made fixes are code like any other code, and they need their own check.

---

## 4. Parallel by default, but split on real seams

Agents are cheap to start and expensive to wait on. When a task has independent parts, such as researching one library while another agent refactors a module, I run them at the same time.

The catch is that each subagent starts with no context. Parallelism pays when the pieces are actually independent, with separate files, separate questions, and a clear interface between them. When the pieces are tangled, splitting them only produces two agents rediscovering the same codebase and merge conflicts at the end. Before splitting work I ask the same question I would ask about splitting a team: where is the seam?

---

## 5. Build for agents as users

This is the change that surprised me most. Once agents are doing real work in your systems, they become users of those systems, and most of our software is hostile to them.

When I reviewed my media server for agent experience, I scored it on discoverability, task shape, determinism, safety, observability, auth, and composability. It had 81 HTTP routes and not one machine-readable description. Playing an episode took five calls, because the API mirrored the UI's steps instead of the user's task. Delete had no dry-run.

The fix improved every experience at once:

- a manifest and OpenAPI spec, so the API describes itself,
- one search endpoint and one `POST /api/play` that goes from title to playable URL in a single call,
- idempotency keys, dry-runs, a read-only token, and an audit log,
- a thin CLI and MCP server on top, so agents and scripts use the same typed layer as the UI.

The UI got simpler because it uses the same task-shaped endpoints. The UI, the developer, and the agent all benefited from one change, because they were all clients of the same underlying API.

This site follows the same idea. Every page has a markdown version, there is an `llms.txt`, and agents can ask it questions directly. If you want software that agents can operate, treat them as a user persona with their own needs, not as an afterthought.

---

## 6. Guardrails belong in config, not vigilance

"I'll watch what it does" does not scale past one agent, and it doesn't hold up at 11pm.

So permissions are written down. Read-only operations such as `kubectl get`, `aws describe-*`, and log tailing are allowed without asking. Mutating ones such as `terraform apply`, `kubectl delete` and `exec`, and anything that creates, deletes, or modifies cloud resources are denied outright or require a prompt. The agent can investigate an incident freely. It cannot change production without me.

One detail matters when you run several tools. They evaluate rules differently. One of my tools uses last-match-wins, so "deny everything, then allow the read-only verbs" works. Another evaluates deny before allow, so the same rules would block everything. When I ported the rules between them, I had to list the mutating verbs explicitly instead. Guardrails are code too, and they need to be checked like code.

---

## What hasn't gotten easier

The factory moves the bottleneck. It does not remove it.

- **Review is now the slow part.** Producing a change is quick. Knowing that it is right is not. That is exactly why the investment goes into tests and verification, not into prompts.
- **Plausible and wrong is the default failure mode.** Agents rarely fail loudly. They write confident code against an API that changed last month. Every rule above is a way of making that kind of failure loud.
- **Taste does not delegate.** An agent can implement a design critique. Deciding what the product should feel like, or which of three reasonable architectures to choose, is still my job.
- **Cold starts are real.** Without written context, each session wastes its first stretch rediscovering things. The session docs and `AGENTS.md` exist to make that stretch shorter.

---

## The point

The home page of this site says I build software that has to keep working after the interesting part is over. Agent-driven development tests that sentence harder than anything else I have done. The interesting part, generating the code, is now nearly free. Everything that makes the code keep working is still engineering, and it is where the work is.

So I build the factory: written context, recorded sessions, tests that replace manual checks, agent-friendly interfaces, and guardrails in config. The features come out of it.

If you are building something similar, I would like to compare notes. Reply by email.

---

# The Myth of Simplicity in Software Systems

2026-03-08 | Tags: SoftwareEngineering, Complexity

![chaos_monkey](/posts/images/simplicity.png)

Software engineers often talk about simplicity as an ideal. We strive to build simple systems, write simple code, and design simple architectures. Simplicity is treated almost like a moral virtue in engineering culture.

Yet if we observe real software systems over time, we see a different pattern. Systems almost always begin simple—and then inevitably become complex.

This is not necessarily a failure of engineering discipline. In many cases, complexity is the natural outcome of solving real problems at scale. Understanding this dynamic is crucial for designing systems that can survive long-term evolution.

---

## The Beginning: Artificial Simplicity

Most systems begin in a state of artificial simplicity.

At the early stages of a project, constraints are minimal:

- a small number of users
- a small codebase
- a single development team
- a limited feature set

In this environment, it is relatively easy to keep the architecture clean. A single application server, a single database, and a handful of services may be enough.

Developers often interpret this early simplicity as proof that the architecture is fundamentally simple. But what they are really observing is a system that has not yet been exposed to real-world pressures.

Over time, those pressures begin to accumulate.

---

## Essential vs Accidental Complexity

Computer scientist Fred Brooks famously distinguished between essential complexity and accidental complexity.

Essential complexity arises from the problem itself.

For example:

- financial systems must handle consistency and transactions
- distributed systems must tolerate network failures
- machine learning infrastructure must handle large datasets and GPU workloads

These complexities are intrinsic to the domain.

Accidental complexity, on the other hand, comes from the tools and abstractions we build around the problem:

- poorly designed frameworks
- unnecessary layers of abstraction
- overengineered architectures

Engineers often believe that if accidental complexity is removed, systems will remain simple. But this overlooks an important reality: essential complexity grows as systems evolve.

A system serving ten users is fundamentally simpler than one serving ten million.

---

## The Microservices Temptation

Few architectural trends illustrate the myth of simplicity better than microservices.

Microservices are often adopted with the promise of simplifying large systems. By decomposing a monolithic application into smaller services, each component becomes easier to reason about.

At least in theory.

In practice, microservices trade one form of complexity for another.

A monolith concentrates complexity within the codebase. Microservices distribute that complexity across the network.

Instead of debugging a function call, engineers must now debug:

- network latency
- service discovery
- distributed tracing
- version mismatches
- partial failures

A simple architecture diagram with five services can conceal a complex operational reality.

This does not mean microservices are inherently bad. In many cases they are the right solution. But they demonstrate a broader lesson: architectural decisions rarely eliminate complexity—they relocate it.

---

## The Problem of Leaky Abstractions

Abstractions are the primary tool engineers use to manage complexity. Programming languages, frameworks, and infrastructure platforms all exist to hide lower-level details.

But abstractions are never perfect.

Joel Spolsky famously described this phenomenon as the Law of Leaky Abstractions: eventually, the underlying complexity reveals itself.

For example:

- ORMs promise to hide SQL, yet developers eventually need to understand database queries.
- Kubernetes abstracts infrastructure, yet operators must still understand networking, storage, and container behavior.
- Serverless platforms hide servers, yet performance and cold-start behavior still matter.

Abstractions are extremely useful, but they cannot eliminate complexity entirely. They merely delay the moment when engineers must confront it.

---

## Conway’s Law and Organizational Complexity

Software systems do not evolve in isolation. They evolve within organizations.

Conway’s Law states:

> Organizations design systems that mirror their communication structure.

This means architecture often reflects team boundaries rather than purely technical considerations.

A small team might maintain a monolith because communication is easy. A large organization with many teams might naturally evolve toward microservices because independent teams need clear ownership boundaries.

As organizations grow, their software systems inherit the complexity of coordination, communication, and decision-making.

In other words, organizational complexity becomes architectural complexity.

---

## The Inevitability of Growth

One of the hardest lessons in software engineering is accepting that complexity is not always avoidable.

A successful system must support:

- more users
- more features
- more integrations
- more engineers contributing to the codebase

Each of these introduces new constraints.

The real challenge is therefore not eliminating complexity but managing its growth.

This requires:

- clear architectural boundaries
- strong observability and debugging tools
- disciplined refactoring
- thoughtful platform design

Without these practices, complexity accumulates silently until the system becomes difficult to change.

---

## Simplicity as a Direction, Not a State

Simplicity in software should not be understood as a permanent condition. It is better thought of as a direction.

Engineers continuously push systems toward simpler designs through refactoring, better abstractions, and improved tooling. But the forces pushing toward complexity never disappear.

New requirements, scale, and organizational change constantly reshape the system.

The goal, therefore, is not to create a system that is permanently simple. The goal is to <strong> build systems that remain understandable even as they grow more complex</strong>.

---

## Further Reading

- [The Mythical Man-Month by Frederick P. Brooks Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month)
- [No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering by Frederick P. Brooks Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Silver_Bullet)
- [The Law of Leaky Abstractions by Joel Spolsky](https://www.joelonsoftware.com/2002/11/11/the-law-of-leaky-abstractions/)
- [Conway's Law by Melvin Conway](https://www.melconway.com/Home/Conways_Law.html)
- [Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann](https://dataintensive.net/)
- [A Philosophy of Software Design by John Ousterhout](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/book.php)

---

# When the System Fights Back: A Journey into Chaos Engineering

2025-01-15 | Tags: DevOps, ChaosEngineering

![chaos_monkey](/posts/images/chaos-monkey.webp)

Let me set the stage. It's Black Friday, and our e-commerce platform is humming along, soaking in the adrenaline of record-breaking traffic. Dashboards were glowing, engineers cautiously sipping their coffee, trying not to jinx the magic. For a moment, it felt like we were invincible.

Then, as if on cue, disaster struck. The error rate graph took a nosedive off a cliff. Orders froze mid-flight. Twitter, the unkindest of mirrors, erupted with complaints. "What now?" Ravi, my perpetually skeptical colleague, asked. His voice carried the weariness of someone who'd seen too many systems fail spectacularly.

The post-mortem wasn't pretty. A cascading failure in an external payment gateway had rippled through our system. The result? A glorified pile-up of transactions waiting for a miracle. "How did we miss this?" someone muttered, and for once, no one had an answer.

"Because," I finally said, "we keep assuming the universe plays fair. Clearly, it doesn't."

Enter chaos engineering - the art of deliberately creating disaster to build stronger systems. I'd read about Netflix's Chaos Monkey, a tool designed to randomly kill servers in production, and I couldn't help but admire the audacity. What if we could turn our system into a fighter - one that could take a punch and still come out swinging?

The heart of chaos engineering lies in controlled chaos. It's not just about breaking things; it's about breaking them with intent. The concept itself is straightforward: you simulate failures in a controlled environment and observe how your system behaves. But here's the catch - it's a lot harder than it sounds.

"So, what? We just... start breaking stuff?" Ravi asked when I pitched the idea.

"Exactly," I said, grinning. "But, you know, scientifically."

![(Image Source: How chaos engineering will guarantee the resilience of your services)](/posts/images/chaos-diagram.webp)

We started with a replica of our production environment - a Kubernetes cluster spinning away like a miniature universe. If Kubernetes is new to you, think of it as an orchestration platform for containers (tiny, self-sufficient environments where your apps run). Within this cluster, we created our sandbox: pods, namespaces, and service meshes ready to face the chaos.

To introduce the madness, I picked Chaos Mesh - a tool that specializes in orchestrating controlled experiments in Kubernetes. It works by defining chaos scenarios in YAML files.

Our first experiment was simple: inject 500ms latency into the payment gateway service. The goal? Test whether our retry mechanisms and circuit breakers would hold up. Here's how it looked in code:

```yaml
apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata:
  name: payment-gateway-latency
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: one
  selector:
    labelSelectors:
      app: payment-gateway
  delay:
    latency: "500ms"
  duration: "30s"
```

When I hit deploy, Ravi leaned in. "So, what happens if this crashes everything?"

"Then we fix it," I said. "And I owe you lunch."

The system initially seemed fine. Hystrix, our circuit breaker library, kicked in like a pro, cutting off failing requests. But then... the unexpected happened. Our retry logic went berserk, spawning an avalanche of redundant requests. Instead of handling the delay gracefully, we'd created a self-inflicted DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service). Ravi just raised an eyebrow and said, "You're really bad at keeping lunch money."

Fixing the fallout was a journey of discovery. First, we revamped our retry logic with exponential backoff - a strategy that makes each retry wait progressively longer, like a kid testing a parent's patience. Then, we fine-tuned our load balancer to handle spikes more gracefully. Finally, we expanded our observability stack, adding metrics for retries, circuit breaker activity, and overall system health.

By the time we ran the experiment again, the system behaved like a seasoned boxer. Latency? No problem. The retries worked without creating chaos, circuit breakers stepped in where needed, and the load balancer handled the traffic without breaking a sweat. Ravi even bought me lunch - though he made me pick the cheapest place in town.

Chaos engineering taught me more than I expected. It's not just a technical exercise; it's a mindset. It's about questioning assumptions, confronting fears, and embracing failure as a teacher. We integrated chaos experiments into our CI/CD pipeline, turning them into regular tests. Post-mortems became celebrations of what we'd learned, rather than finger-pointing sessions. And our systems? Stronger than ever.

But chaos engineering isn't just about the tech. It's about the culture you build around it. It's about teaching your team to think like detectives, to dig into logs and metrics with curiosity instead of dread. It's about laughing at the absurdity of breaking things on purpose and marveling at how much you learn when you do.

So here's my challenge to you: embrace the chaos. Whether you're running a small app or a massive platform, the principles hold true. Build your gladiator arena, unleash the chaos, and watch your system evolve. It's scary, sure. But it's also exhilarating. _Because resilience isn't something you stumble into - it's something you engineer, one glorious failure at a time._

## Further Reading:

- [Principles of Chaos Engineering (The Official Site)](https://principlesofchaos.org/)
- [Breaking Things on Purpose Podcast by Gremlin](https://www.gremlin.com/podcast)
- [The Netflix Tech Blog: Chaos Engineering](https://netflixtechblog.com/tagged/chaos-engineering)
- [A Guide to Chaos Engineering with Kubernetes](https://opensource.com/article/21/5/kubernetes-chaos)
- [Resilience Engineering and Chaos (InfoQ)](http://www.infoq.com/chaos-engineering/)
- [O'Reilly: Chaos Engineering Book](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/chaos-engineering/9781492043850/)

---

# Introduction to Golang

2024-06-01 | Tags: 60DaysOfLearning2024, LearningWithLeapfrog, Go

## Introduction

**This is a part of #60DaysOfLearning challenge by Leapfrog.**

I want to start my journey with DevOps. So, I am starting with learning Go. I will explore Go in depth for this week and move on to more tools.

Go has become a de facto language for cloud orchestration and software in the larger world.(from Kubernetes to Docker). I used to do Python. But seems like Python has some problems at scale, from running out of memory to The Global Interpreter Lock|(GIL) preventing true multi threading. And, the runtime errors due to dynamic typing are a bit of pain.

This is a collection of things I learned today.

This post assumes you have knowledge of at least one programming language, preferably C and/or Python.

## Package Management

Go divides programs into packages, and all go files in a directory must belong to the same package.

Declaring a package is as simple as the following:

```go
package main
```

`package main` is special. All other package names declare a package that must be imported into another package to be used. Package main will declare `func main()`, which is the starting point for a binary to run.

Let's say you have a directory structure as follows:

```go
mypackage/
	file1.go
	file2.go
```

Then, `file1.go` and `file2.go` should have the following:

```go
package main
```

When `mypackage` is imported by another package, it will include everything declared in all files in the `mypackage` directory.

To import a package, you basically have two general types.Standard library packages stand out because they don't list some repository information in their path, such as the following:

```go
"fmt"
"encoding/json"
"archive/zip"
```

All other packages generally have repository information preceding them, as follows:

```go
"github.com/johnsiilver/golib/lru"
"github.com/kylelemons/godebug/pretty"
```

And every imported package must be used at least once, otherwise if you need to do a _side effects_ import, in which just loading the package causes something to happen, but you don't use the package. This should always be done in package main and requires prepending with an underscore (`_`):

```go
package main
import (
  "fmt"
  _ "github.com/kylelemons/godebug/pretty"//Just an example
)
func main() {
 fmt.Println("Hello, playground")
}
```

## A basic Hello World program

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	hello := "Hello World!"
	fmt.Println(hello)
}
```

Here := means create a variable and assign the string value to it. You could use `var hello` to just initialize. Go syntax is similar to C and scopes are defined with curly braces.

## Zero Values

In some older languages, a variable declaration without an assignment has an unknown value. This is because the program creates a place in memory to store the value but doesn't put anything in it. So, the bits representing the value are set to whatever happened to be in that memory space before you created the variable. But in Go, declaring a variable without an assignment automatically assigns a value called the _zero value_.

![Zero Values in Go](/posts/images/intro-to-go.png)

## Function/statement variable should be used

The rule here is that if you create a variable within a function or statement, it must be used. This is much for the same reason as package imports; declaring a variable that isn't used is almost always a mistake.

This can be relaxed in much the same way as an import, using `_`.

```go
_ = someVar
```

## Looping, Branching, and Functions

As it is just some syntactical changes, I will not be discussing these in the post.

However, as in Python, functions in Go supports multiple variables to return.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func divide(num, div int) (res, rem int) {
	result = num / div
	remainder = num % div
	return res, rem
}

func main() {
	result, remainder := divide(3, 2)
	fmt.Printf("Result: %d, Remainder %d", result, remainder)
}
```

### Varidac Arguments

A _variadic argument_ is when you want to provide 0 to infinite arguments. A good example would be calculating a sum of integers.

Here is an example:

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func sum(nums ...int) {
    total := 0
    for _, num := range nums {
        total += num
    }
    fmt.Println(total)
}

func main() {
    sum(1, 2)
    sum(1, 2, 3)
}

```

In this example, `nums` is a slice of integers. The `range` keyword is used to iterate over each element of the `nums` .

### Anonymous Functions

Go has a concept of **anonymous functions**, which means a function without a name (also called a function closure).

```go
func main() {
	result := func(word1, word2 string) string {
							return word1 + " " + word2
				 }("hello", "world")
	fmt.Println(result)
}
```

### Defining Private and Public

Just remember a rule: To be public, the constant/variable/function/method must simply start with an uppercase letter. If it starts with a lowercase letter, it is private.

## Structures, Methods and Pointers

Go supports the use of pointers, as every call to a function is call by value, it is necessary. However, in most use cases, we need not go overboard with pointers. Structures and methods are defined as the code example below.

```go
type Record struct{
 Name string
 Age int
}
// a method for the struct
func (r Record) String() string {
 return fmt.Sprintf("%s,%d", r.Name, r.Age)
}
```

And, Go doesn't provide any specialized code for that, instead, we use a constructor pattern using simple functions.

```go
func NewRecord(name string, age int) (*Record, error) {
	if name == "" {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("name cannot be the empty string")
	}
	if age <= 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("age cannot be <= 0")
	}
	return &Record{Name: name, Age: age}, nil
}
```

This can be then implemented in code as:

```go
rec, err := NewRecord("John Doak", 100)
 if err != nil {
 return err
}
```

We will explore errors in the coming days.

## Understanding Interface in GO

In Go, an interface is a set of method signatures. When a type provides the definition for all the methods in the interface, it is said to implement the interface. It provides a way to achieve runtime polymorphism. An interface can be defined using the `type` keyword, followed by the name of the interface and the `interface` keyword.

Here is an example:

```go
type Writer interface {
	Write([]byte) (int, error)
}

```

In this example, any type that defines a method `Write` with the exact signature is said to satisfy the `Writer` interface. Interfaces can be embedded in other interfaces to create composite interfaces.

```go
type Reader interface {
	Read([]byte) (int, error)
}

type Writer interface {
	Write([]byte) (int, error)
}

type ReadWriter interface {
	Reader
	Writer
}

```

In this case, any type that satisfies both `Reader` and `Writer` interfaces satisfies the `ReadWriter` interface. Remember, Go interfaces are implemented implicitly, so there's no need to explicitly declare that a type implements an interface.

## Conclusion

As we've explored in this post, understanding Go's package management, functions, loops, and interfaces provides a solid foundation for diving deeper into the language in the further days. Feel free to suggest changes in the article and look out for more posts.

1. **Packages:** every file in a directory belongs to one package.
2. **Zero values:** uninitialized variables are still valid.
3. **Short declarations:** `:=` keeps local code concise.
4. **Interfaces:** implemented implicitly, no extra keywords.

## Practical examples

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func divide(num, div int) (int, int) {
  return num / div, num % div
}

func main() {
  result, remainder := divide(3, 2)
  fmt.Printf("Result: %d, Remainder: %d\n", result, remainder)
}
```

```go
type Writer interface {
  Write([]byte) (int, error)
}
```

## Takeaway

Go gives you enough abstraction to move fast and enough constraints to avoid accidental complexity. For systems work, that balance is a huge advantage.
